unit.title: Disconnect and reconnect fixed wired electrical machinery appliance and fixtures

summary: This unit teaches you to plan and lead the safe disconnection and reconnection of fixed-wired equipment: water heaters, air-conditioners, pumps, motors, cookers, fans and light fittings. You will learn to isolate and prove dead, deal with stored energy, record connections, make disconnected ends safe, check that new equipment suits the circuit, reconnect to the maker's instructions, test before and after the supply is restored, and keep the records.

blocks.p: Fixed-wired equipment is connected straight to the building's wiring instead of through a plug: water heaters, air-conditioners, pumps, motors and machines, cookers, ceiling fans, exhaust fans and light fittings. It has to be disconnected when it is repaired, moved or replaced, and reconnected afterwards. Done badly, this work leaves live ends in ceilings, motors turning the wrong way, heaters on cables too small for them and machines whose cases are not earthed. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who plan the work, lead a small team, do the calculations, test the result and keep the records.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the job
Read the work order and the nameplates, survey the site, check the circuit, agree a time with the users, arrange the other trades and write a short method statement with hold points.
Isolate and control stored energy
Lock off at the right isolator (with a hasp for a team), prove dead between every pair of conductors, and allow for capacitors, hot parts, turning parts, water and refrigerant.
Record the connections
Photograph, sketch and label every conductor and link before anything is taken off.
Disconnect and make safe
Take the conductors off in a safe order and leave every end insulated, enclosed and labelled, for a short time or for good.
Remove and handle the equipment
Plan the lift, support the weight, and deal properly with the old equipment, tubes and waste.
Check new equipment against the circuit
Compare voltage, frequency, phases and current with the supply, breaker and cable; work out currents, resistances and voltage drop; decide whether the circuit must be upgraded.
Reconnect to the maker's instructions
Earth first, the right terminals and links, the maker's torque, glands and grips holding the sheath, and covers, seals and guards refitted.
Test and return to service
Inspect, carry out dead tests, have the supply restored by the authorised person, check the function (including a motor's rotation) and hand over.
Lead and record
Brief and supervise the team, check work at hold points, and complete the isolation, connection and test records and the circuit chart.

head: Equipment
Usual supply
Points to watch
rows: Tank water heater
220 V from a two-pole breaker; often 3 to 4.5 kW
Must be full of water before it is switched on; treated as a continuous load; the plumber drains and refills it.
Split air-conditioner
Usually 220 V (some small units 110 V), with an outdoor isolator
Capacitors and inverter boards hold a charge; refrigerant is work for a certified technician; the nameplate gives the largest breaker allowed.
Water pump or pressure set
110 V or 220 V single-phase; three-phase on large sets
Wet places, a capacitor, the direction of rotation, and pressure or float switch wiring.
Motor on a machine
Single-phase or three-phase, through a starter with an overload relay
Terminal links, overload setting, rotation, guards and weight.
Electric cooker or range
110/220 V: two lines, a neutral and an earth
Heavy; four conductors; large cable.
Ceiling fans and light fittings
Usually 110 V lighting circuits
Weight must be supported; the switch must break the line; shared neutrals; old tubes contain mercury.

blocks.note: JPS supplies most buildings at **110/220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**: two lines, each about 110 V to neutral and to earth, and about 220 V between them. Factories and large buildings may also have a three-phase supply. Much equipment sold in Jamaica is made for the US market at **115/230 V, 60 Hz**, so always read the nameplate for frequency as well as voltage. A new or altered circuit may need inspection by a licensed electrical inspector under the Government Electrical Regulator (GER) before it is connected; your supervisor will tell you when this applies.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The sections follow a real job, from planning to handover. You already know safe isolation and testing from your earlier units; here you apply them to fixed equipment and take charge of the job. Finding faults inside the equipment itself is a separate unit. Read the notes, then do the practice test and read every explanation.

Most problems in this work start before anyone picks up a screwdriver: the new heater is too big for the cable, the plumber is not booked, the hotel was not told its guests would have no hot water, or the replacement motor is the wrong type. A Level 3 electrician prevents these by planning.

ul: **Read the work order**: what is to be disconnected, why, and what replaces it.
**Read the nameplate and the maker's installation instructions** for the new equipment: supply, current, largest breaker, cable entries, fixing, clearances and isolator.
**Survey the site**: which board and breaker feed the equipment, the cable route, the local isolator, access (ladder, tower), the weight and the route out, and what other trades are needed.
**Check the existing circuit against the new load** (see 'Checking the new equipment and the circuit'). If it must be upgraded, plan and order the cable, breaker and isolator.
**Agree the time** with the owner or manager, so the users can plan for being without water, cooling, lights or the machine. Hotels, clinics, farms and restaurants need notice.

**Arrange the other trades**: a plumber to drain and refill a water heater or uncouple a pump, a certified refrigeration technician for an air-conditioner, a fitter for couplings, belts and alignment.
**Check that the replacement is what the work order says.** If it is a different type or rating, stop and check with your supervisor and the customer before you fit it.

blocks.h: The method statement and hold points

blocks.p: Write a short **method statement**: the steps in order, who does each one, where the isolation points are, the tests, and the **hold points**. A hold point is a step where the work stops until the leader has checked it. Typical hold points on a disconnect-and-reconnect job:

flow: Isolation and proving dead, watched by the leader
Connection record checked, before anything is disconnected
Reconnection checked, before covers go on
Dead test results checked, before the supply is restored

head: Item
Why you need it
rows: Two-pole voltage tester and its proving unit
To prove dead at the point of work, with the tester checked before and after.
Multi-lock hasp, a personal padlock for each person, danger tags
So each person controls their own safety.
Phone or camera, notebook, labels or marker tape
To record every connection before it is removed.
Insulated connectors, junction boxes with lids, blanking plates
To make disconnected ends safe.
Torque screwdriver and the maker's torque figures
To tighten terminals correctly.
Low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
For the dead tests after reconnection.
Capacitor discharge tool (a resistor in an insulated holder)
For stored charge in motors and air-conditioners.
Lifting aids, slings, a second person, safe access equipment
For heavy or high equipment.
Dust sheets, a vacuum, bags and tube cartons
To leave the site clean and to keep old tubes whole.

blocks.note: Take more photographs than you think you need: the whole terminal box, then each terminal close up, with the labels showing. A photo costs nothing; guessing a connection later can wreck a motor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The isolation rules are the same as for any electrical work. Fixed equipment adds its own problems: two-pole and three-phase supplies, more than one source, control wiring fed from somewhere else, and energy that stays after the supply is off.

head: Situation
Isolate at
rows: Equipment with a lockable local isolator (disconnect) beside it
The local isolator, locked off. Lock the breaker at the board as well where the procedure says, for example when the isolator is outdoors where the public can reach it.
Equipment fed straight from a breaker
The breaker, locked with a breaker lockout device.
A machine with a starter
The isolator before the starter. **Never** rely on the stop button, the emergency stop or the control fuse: they do not cut the main supply, and anyone can reset them.
A 220 V circuit
A **two-pole** breaker or isolator that opens both lines together. Each line is about 110 V to earth, so switching off one line leaves the other live.
Three-phase equipment
A three-pole isolator or breaker that opens all three lines.

blocks.p: When several people work on the same equipment, lock the isolator with a **multi-lock hasp**. Each person fits their own padlock and keeps the key; the leader fixes the danger tag. The supply cannot be restored until the last lock is off. If you come back to the job and the tag is missing or something has been moved, refit the tag and prove dead again before you carry on.

blocks.h: Prove dead at the point of work

flow: Prove the tester on the proving unit
Test at the equipment's terminals between every pair of conductors, earth included
Only now treat the equipment as dead

head: Supply
Test between
rows: 110 V single-phase (L, N, E)
L and N
L and E
N and E
220 V with no neutral (L1, L2, E)
L1 and L2
L1 and E
L2 and E
110/220 V with a neutral (L1, L2, N, E), such as a cooker
L1 and L2
Each line and N
Each line and E
N and E
Three-phase (L1, L2, L3, E, and N if there is one)
Each line and each other line
Each line and E (and N)
N and E

ul: **Control wiring from another circuit.** A pump's float switch, a machine's control panel or an air-conditioner's thermostat wiring may be fed from a different board. Test every terminal in the box, not just the main ones.

**Shared (borrowed) neutrals.** In older wiring, two circuits sometimes share one neutral. With your circuit off, that neutral can still carry current from the other circuit. When you open it, the end connected to the other circuit's loads becomes live. Find and isolate both circuits.
**Standby generators, solar PV and battery inverters, UPS units.** Find and isolate every source.
**Equipment fed through another panel.** A machine may get its supply or interlocks through another machine. Check the drawings.

head: Energy
Where you meet it
How to control it
rows: Electrical charge
Run and start capacitors in motors, fans and air-conditioners; the large DC capacitors on inverter boards and variable speed drives

Wait the time printed on the label (often 5 to 15 minutes for inverter boards), then measure the voltage across the capacitor; discharge it with a proper resistor tool if needed. Never short it with a screwdriver.
Movement
Motors, fans and pumps running down after switch-off; fan blades turned by the wind
Wait until everything has stopped; block or tie fan blades that the wind can turn.
Heat
Heater elements, hot water in a tank, motors that were running
Allow to cool; have hot water drained before anything is opened.
Pressure
Water in pumps and heaters; refrigerant in air-conditioners
The plumber isolates and drains the water; only a certified technician deals with refrigerant.
Weight and springs
Heavy fittings and fans, raised parts, spring returns
Support the weight before the fixings are removed.

blocks.note: A capacitor can hold a charge long after the supply is off, and a shock on a ladder can throw you off it. Treat every capacitor as charged until you have measured it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before you take anything off, make a record good enough for someone else to reconnect the equipment correctly from it alone. Then disconnect in a safe order and leave nothing live, bare or hidden.

ul: **Photographs**: the whole terminal box or connection area, then each terminal close up, with the conductor labels showing.
**A labelled sketch** (connection diagram): every terminal, the conductor that lands on it (its colour and label), and every link or bridge.
**A label on each conductor** as it is removed, naming the terminal it came off (for example L1, L2, N, PE, U1, T4, 'thermostat 2').
**The nameplate details**: voltage, frequency, phases, power or current, and the connection (for example Δ or Y on a motor).
**The circuit**: board, breaker number and rating, cable size and type, isolator.

head: Marking
Meaning
rows: L, L1, L2 (black or red; 'hot')
Line conductors
N (white or grey)
Neutral
PE, E, G or the earth symbol (green, green and yellow, or bare)
Protective earth: the equipment grounding conductor
U1, V1, W1 and U2, V2, W2
The two ends of each of the three windings of a three-phase motor (IEC marking)
T1, T2, T3 and so on
Motor leads under the US (NEMA) system: T1 to T6 on many star-delta and dual-voltage motors, T1 to T9 on nine-lead motors
U1, U2 and Z1, Z2
Main winding and auxiliary (start) winding of many single-phase motors made to IEC standards
A1, A2
The coil of a contactor or relay
The normally closed contact of an overload relay, wired into the control circuit

blocks.p: **Links** in a motor terminal box decide how the windings are connected to suit the supply: in **star (Y)** or **delta (Δ)** on a three-phase motor, or in **series** or **parallel** on a dual-voltage motor. Record their exact positions before you remove them. Never trust conductor colours alone; old work and imported equipment use different colours. Your record and your labels are what count.

flow: Isolated, locked, tagged and proved dead
Record made and checked by the leader (hold point)

blocks.p: The earth is **disconnected last** and **connected first** for the same reason: the metal case must stay earthed whenever a line conductor could be connected to it. If a line were still live from another source, or the supply were restored by mistake, the earthed case lets the fault current trip the breaker instead of leaving the case live.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Equipment removed for a short time (repair, or a replacement next week)
Keep the circuit isolated, locked and tagged, with the reason on the tag
Fit each conductor end with a suitable insulated connector
Put the ends in a junction box or the existing enclosure, with its lid on
Label them: circuit number, 'equipment removed, circuit isolated'
Equipment removed for good
Disconnect the circuit at the board
Remove the breaker, or mark it SPARE; fit a blank where a gap is left in the cover
Take the cable out, or terminate it in connectors in an accessible box with a lid at both ends, and label it
Update the circuit chart
A light fitting removed and not replaced
Ends in connectors in a box with a lid or a blank plate at the ceiling, labelled. Never leave ends loose in the ceiling space.

blocks.note: Never leave bare ends, ends wrapped only in tape, ends pushed into a wall or ceiling, or a cable cut flush and plastered over. Someone may switch the circuit on, or drill into it, years later. Every joint and termination must stay in a box with a cover that can be reached.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Opening old installations often shows hidden problems. Put right, and report, what you find: a joint wrapped only in tape inside a ceiling is remade in a proper box; brittle or cracked insulation near a lamp holder or heater is cut back to sound cable, or the cable is replaced; a missing earth is reported and fixed before anything is reconnected. Write each one on the job record and tell the customer.
Many fixed items are heavy, awkward or high up, and some hold water, oil, refrigerant or hazardous materials. Plan the removal as carefully as the electrical work.

head: Item
Plan for
rows: Tank water heater
The plumber turns off the water and drains the tank. A full 150-litre (40-gallon) heater weighs about 200 kg, and the water may be hot enough to scald, so it is never moved full.
Pump and motor

The fitter uncouples the pump and the pipes are drained. Lift with two people, a lifting aid, or the motor's **eye bolt**: screwed fully home, and used to lift the motor alone, never the motor and pump together.
Air-conditioner
A certified technician pumps down or recovers the refrigerant before any pipe is undone. Outdoor units are heavy and often high on walls.
Ceiling fan or heavy light fitting
Support the weight (a second person, or the hook on the fan bracket) before the fixings come out. Never let it hang on its conductors.
Machine
Guards, sharp edges, oil and heavy castings. Use the maker's lifting points.

ul: Find the weight (nameplate or maker's data), plan the route, doors and stairs, and where the item will be put down.

Use two people or a lifting aid (trolley, hoist, chain block) for anything heavy or awkward. About 25 kg is often taken as a guide for one person lifting close to the body at waist height, and much less when reaching, twisting or working above the shoulders.
Keep your back straight, the load close and your feet apart; do not twist while lifting.
Never take the weight of a fitting or fan while standing on a ladder: use a tower or platform, with a second person.

head: Waste
How to deal with it
rows: Fluorescent tubes and compact fluorescent lamps
They contain mercury. Keep them whole, pack them in their boxes or a tube carton, and send them for proper disposal through an approved route. Never break them into a skip.
Old ballasts and capacitors
Very old ones (made before about 1980) may contain PCBs, a toxic oil. If one is leaking, do not touch the oil: bag it, label it and report it.
Old appliances and motors
Return them to the customer, take them for recycling, or dispose of them as agreed in writing. Never leave them outside the door, take them for yourself or dump them.
Cable off-cuts and packaging
Bag and remove them. Copper scrap goes back to the store as the Centre's procedure says.

blocks.note: Old appliances and tubes dumped in gullies block drains, cause flooding in the rainy season and poison water. Agree what happens to the old equipment before the job starts and write it on the job card.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Checking the new equipment and the circuit

blocks.p: The most common serious mistake in this work is connecting new equipment to a circuit that cannot carry it. At Level 3 you do the checks and the sums yourself, and you stop the job if they show a problem.

head: Nameplate item
What to check
rows: Voltage
It must match the supply. Equipment marked 230 V normally works on 220 V. A 110 V item must never go on 220 V; a 220 V item on 110 V will not work properly, and a motor may burn out.
Frequency (50 Hz, 60 Hz or 50/60 Hz)

Jamaica is 50 Hz. Check 60 Hz-only equipment with the maker before fitting it. A 60 Hz motor on 50 Hz runs about one-sixth slower, and at the same voltage it carries more magnetic flux, draws more current and can overheat. Timers and clocks that count mains cycles run slow.
Phases
Single-phase or three-phase, to match the supply.
Power (W, kW) or current (A, FLA, FLC)
Use it to work out the current and compare it with the breaker and the cable.
MCA and MOP (on air-conditioners and similar)
MCA is the minimum circuit ampacity: the cable must be rated for at least this. MOP is the maximum overcurrent protection ('max fuse' or 'max breaker'): the breaker must not be larger.
IP rating, weight, clearances
Suitable for the place (outdoors, wet areas); the fixing can carry the weight; the maker's spaces for air and service are kept.

head: To find
Formula
Example
rows: Current from power
I = P ÷ V
Power from voltage and current
P = V × I
Resistance of a heater element
R = V² ÷ P
Power from resistance
P = V² ÷ R
Total current of several items
Add the watts, then divide by the voltage
Change in current
New current minus old current
Voltage drop in a cable
VD = I × 2 × L × r (both conductors: out and back)

blocks.note: Nickel-chrome heater wire changes its resistance by only a few per cent as it heats, so a cold element reads close to its working value. A filament lamp is different: cold, it reads far less than when it is lit.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Compare the new current with three things: the **breaker**, the **cable's current rating** and the **voltage drop**. The usual limits for copper cable in ordinary conditions under the NEC-based code are:

head: Copper conductor
Usual largest breaker
rows: 14 AWG (about 2.1 mm²)
12 AWG (about 3.3 mm²)
10 AWG (about 5.3 mm²)
8 AWG (about 8.4 mm²)
40 A for common house cable; more for some cable types

blocks.p: A long run, a hot roof space, cables bunched together and aluminium conductors all reduce what a cable can carry. For voltage drop, a common design aim is no more than about **3%** on a branch circuit (and 5% in total from the meter). Use the code tables and your supervisor's design for the final choice.

A load that can run for three hours or more is a **continuous load**. Under the NEC-based code the circuit for a continuous load is sized at not less than **125%** of its current, and a fixed storage water heater is treated as continuous. Example: a 4,500 W, 220 V heater draws 20.5 A; 20.5 × 1.25 = 25.6 A, so it needs a 30 A two-pole breaker and cable rated for 30 A (10 AWG copper). A 20 A circuit is too small.

blocks.note: **Never fit a bigger breaker to suit a bigger load without upgrading the cable.** The breaker is there to protect the cable. A 30 A breaker on 12 AWG cable would let the cable overheat inside the wall without tripping.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **The local isolator**: rated for the current, lockable, two-pole for 220 V, within sight of the equipment and, outdoors, weatherproof (for example IP65 or NEMA 3R).
**Protection**: GFCI protection where the code or the maker requires it; some equipment needs an **RCBO** (residual current breaker with overcurrent protection).
**Earthing**: an equipment grounding conductor runs all the way to the equipment.
**Entries and terminals**: the glands suit the cable, and the terminals take the conductor size.
**Fixings**: brackets and the wall or ceiling can carry the weight.

blocks.note: If the new equipment is not what the work order says, or your sums show the circuit is too small, **stop** and tell your supervisor and the customer. Explain the choices in plain words: upgrade the circuit, or choose equipment that suits the circuit there now.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Reconnect with the supply still isolated and locked off, working from your connection record and the maker's instructions.

flow: Check the isolation is still in place
Bring the cable in through the right gland or entry
Connect the neutral, if there is one

head: Point
Standard
rows: Stripping
Strip only as much insulation as the terminal needs: no bare copper outside the terminal and no insulation under the screw. Do not nick the conductor.
Stranded conductors

All strands inside the terminal. Use a crimped bootlace ferrule on fine-stranded conductors in screw-clamp terminals. Do not tin the ends with solder: solder creeps under the screw and the joint works loose.
Tightness
Tighten to the maker's **torque** with a torque screwdriver. Too loose, and the joint heats and arcs; too tight, and the conductor or terminal is damaged.
Cable entry
The sheath goes **inside** the gland or cord grip, so the grip holds the sheath and not the cores. Fit a **grommet** or bush where a cable passes through sheet metal.
Routing
Keep conductors clear of elements, hot surfaces and moving parts; leave a little slack; do not strain the terminals.
Earth
To the terminal marked for earth, with its own screw; never under a cover or fixing screw that may be removed later.
Outdoors
Weatherproof glands, a drip loop so water runs off, seals refitted and every hole sealed.

blocks.p: If a new route goes through a wall, make the hole no bigger than needed, sleeve it, and seal it. If the wall is a fire barrier, fire-stop the hole with an approved material. Seal outdoor entries so that water, insects and lizards cannot get in. Any joint needed to extend a cable is made with proper connectors in a box with a cover that stays accessible.

head: Task
How
rows: Set the links to suit the supply

Read the nameplate. A three-phase motor marked 230 V Δ / 400 V Y is connected in **delta** on a 230 V supply and in **star** on a 400 V supply. A dual-voltage single-phase motor (for example 115/230 V) has its main winding halves in **parallel** for the lower voltage and in **series** for the higher one. Follow the diagram on the plate or inside the cover.
Set the overload relay

Normally to the motor's nameplate **full-load current (FLC)** for the connection used. Some codes and makers allow a little more for motors with a service factor above 1.0. Never turn it up to stop trips.
Check the direction of rotation

Pumps, fans and compressors can be damaged by running backwards. The authorised person (at the Centre, the instructor) gives a very short start, the **bump test**, with guards on and people clear, and watches the shaft or the arrow on the casing.
Correct wrong rotation

Isolate first. On a three-phase motor, swap **any two** of the three lines at the motor or starter. On a single-phase motor, reverse the start (auxiliary) winding connections as the maker's diagram shows; some cannot be reversed.
Re-align and guard
The fitter re-aligns couplings and belts, and every guard goes back before the motor runs.

ul: A metal-bodied fitting has its earth terminal connected to the circuit's protective conductor. If there is no protective conductor at the box, one must be provided before a metal fitting is fixed.
The switch breaks the **line**, never the neutral. On an Edison-screw lamp holder the centre contact goes to the switched line and the screw shell to the neutral.
A ceiling fan hangs from a box or bracket made and marked for fan support and fixed to the structure, never from an ordinary light-fitting box.
When fluorescent fittings are changed to LED, follow the instructions for that type: some LED tubes need the ballast removed and the lamp holders rewired. Label converted fittings.
Check whether a lighting circuit shares a neutral with another circuit, and isolate both.

blocks.p: Testing proves that what you have connected is safe before anyone switches it on. The order matters: inspect, test dead, then energise, then test the function.

flow: Tools out; covers and guards on
Each person removes their own lock; tag removed
Authorised person restores the supply, everyone clear

ul: The right equipment, connected as the record and the maker's diagram show; links set for the supply.
Terminals tight, no bare copper outside them, no loose strands; earth connected.
Glands, grips, covers, seals and guards in place; outdoor entries sealed.
Isolator correct and labelled; no tools, off-cuts or screws left inside.

head: Test
What it shows
Typical result
rows: Continuity of the protective conductor (earth)
The metal parts are connected to the earth at the board, so a fault will trip the breaker
Very low: usually well under 1 Ω, depending on cable size and length. Compare with what you expect for that run.
Insulation resistance (IR)
No leakage between conductors, or from conductors to earth

Tested at 500 V DC on 110/220 V circuits. At least 1 MΩ is the usual minimum; new work normally reads far higher. Disconnect or protect electronic parts (inverter boards, LED drivers, electronic controls) first.
Polarity
Switches, fuses and single-pole devices are in the line; an Edison-screw centre contact is on the line
Correct at every point.
Element or winding resistance, where useful
The heater or motor circuit is complete and not shorted
Close to the value worked out (R = V² ÷ P) or given by the maker.

blocks.h: Restoring the supply and testing the function

ul: Only when every lock has been removed by its owner, and everyone is clear, does the **authorised person** restore the supply. At the Centre this is the instructor.
A water heater must be **full of water** before it is switched on. An element powered dry burns out in seconds.
Motors: a bump test for rotation first, then a run, with the running current measured by the authorised person and compared with the nameplate.
Air-conditioners: the technician checks the refrigerant side; the running current is compared with the nameplate.
Test any GFCI with its test button, and check that thermostats, controls, stops and interlocks work.

blocks.p: Explain to the owner or operator what was done, show the equipment working, point out the isolator and any new controls, give any advice (for example 'never switch the heater on after plumbing work until the tank has been refilled'), and get their signature on the job record.

blocks.note: Only the person who fitted a lock removes it. If a lock is left on and its owner has gone home, the supervisor follows the Centre's procedure. Never cut someone else's lock off.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Leading the team and keeping records

ul: Brief the team from the method statement: the job, the risks, the isolation, who does what, the hold points, and everyone's right to stop the work if something looks unsafe.
Match tasks to each trainee's skill, and pair a less experienced trainee with a stronger one.
Watch the isolation and the proving dead yourself.
At each hold point, check the work before the next step starts. If you find a fault, such as ends left bare and unlabelled, stop the work, have it put right at once and explain why.
Note what each trainee did, for their training record.

head: Record
What it holds
Why it matters
rows: Isolation record
Which isolator, who locked off, when, and when the locks came off
Shows the work was done safely.
Connection record
Photos, sketch, labels, link positions
Lets the equipment be reconnected correctly and checked later.
Equipment details
Old and new nameplates; changes to cable, breaker or isolator
Shows the equipment suits the circuit.
Test record
Dead test results and function test, with the instrument used
Shows it was safe before switch-on, and gives a baseline for later tests.
Circuit chart
Each breaker, its rating and what it feeds
So the next person isolates the right circuit; it must show the true load and breaker.
Job record and handover
Who received the equipment, advice given, anything still to do, materials and time
Protects the customer, the team and the Centre.

blocks.note: A useful record is specific: '4.5 kW heater fitted; circuit upgraded to 30 A two-pole breaker and 10 AWG cable; IR over 200 MΩ; earth continuity 0.35 Ω; handed to Mrs Brown at 3:15 p.m.' tells the next electrician far more than 'heater changed'.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can plan a disconnect-and-reconnect job: work order, nameplates, survey, users told, other trades booked, method statement and hold points.
I can choose the right isolation point for fixed equipment and explain why a stop button, emergency stop or control fuse is not isolation.
I can lead a group isolation with a hasp and prove dead between every pair of conductors on 110 V, 220 V, 110/220 V and three-phase supplies.
I can find other sources, including control wiring and shared neutrals, and control stored energy in capacitors, moving parts, heat, water and weight.
I can record connections with photos, a labelled sketch, conductor labels and link positions.
I can disconnect in a safe order, earth last, and make the ends safe for a short time or for good.
I can plan the safe removal of heavy equipment and deal properly with old equipment, tubes and waste.
I can read a nameplate, including frequency, MCA and MOP, and say whether new equipment suits the supply.
I can work out current, power, element resistance, changes in load and voltage drop, and apply the 125% rule for continuous loads.
I can decide whether a circuit's breaker and cable must be upgraded, and explain why a bigger breaker alone is dangerous.
I can reconnect earth first, to the maker's torque, with the sheath held in the gland or grip.
I can set motor links for the supply, set the overload to the full-load current and arrange a rotation check.
I can connect light fittings and fans with the switch in the line, the earth connected and the weight properly supported.
I can carry out and record the dead tests, and explain who restores the supply and when.
I can hand over the equipment and complete the isolation, connection and test records and the circuit chart.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: The JPS single-phase supply; each line is about 110 V to earth
I = P ÷ V; R = V² ÷ P
Current from power; element resistance from its rating
Circuit size for a continuous load, such as a storage water heater
Usual largest breakers for 14 / 12 / 10 AWG copper
About 3%
A common design aim for voltage drop on a branch circuit
500 V DC, at least 1 MΩ
Usual insulation resistance test voltage and minimum for 110/220 V circuits
About one-sixth slower
A 60 Hz motor run on Jamaica's 50 Hz supply

terms: Bump test
A very short start of a motor to see which way it turns, given by the authorised person.
Continuous load
A load that can run for three hours or more; its circuit is sized at 125% of its current.
Connection record
Photos, a labelled sketch and conductor labels showing exactly how equipment was connected.
Dead tests
Tests done with the supply off: earth continuity, insulation resistance and polarity.
Eye bolt
A threaded ring screwed into the top of a motor for lifting the motor alone.
Fixed-wired equipment
Equipment connected straight to the fixed wiring, not through a plug.
Full-load current (FLC)
The current a motor draws at its rated output, shown on the nameplate; the usual overload setting.
Hold point
A step where work stops until the leader has checked it.
Isolator (disconnect)
A lockable switch near the equipment that cuts off its supply for work.
Links
Bars or jumpers in a terminal box that set how motor windings are connected: star or delta, series or parallel.
MCA / MOP
Minimum circuit ampacity (smallest cable rating) and maximum overcurrent protection (largest breaker) on a nameplate.
RCBO
Residual current breaker with overcurrent protection: earth leakage and overcurrent protection in one device.
Shared (borrowed) neutral
A neutral used by two circuits; it can be live when only one circuit is isolated.
Stored energy
Energy left after the supply is off: charged capacitors, moving parts, heat, pressure and weight.
Torque
The turning force, given by the maker, to which a terminal screw is tightened.
Voltage drop
The voltage lost along a cable because of its resistance: current × loop resistance.

c1.title: A new pump motor at an Ewarton poultry farm
c1.text: Mr Clifton Gayle's poultry farm near Ewarton, St Catherine, pumps water from a storage tank to the chicken houses. The pump's single-phase motor has burnt out. It is fed at 220 V from a 20 A two-pole breaker through a lockable isolator beside the pump. Trainee leader Tashoya and two trainees are to fit a replacement motor. The motor in the supplier's box has a nameplate reading: 115/230 V, 60 Hz, 1 phase, 1.5 hp, FLA 16.4/8.2 A. The burnt-out motor's plate read 110/220 V, 50 Hz. The birds need water every few hours in the heat.

c2.title: A cook shop refit in Falmouth
c2.text: Miss Hyacinth Morgan's cook shop in Falmouth, Trelawny, is being refitted. The old 220 V fixed-wired fryer on circuit 7 (a 30 A two-pole breaker) is being removed for good, because a gas range is replacing it. The 110 V exhaust fan above the fryer, on circuit 9, is to move 2 m along the same wall. Trainee Kemoy locks off circuit 9, proves dead at the fan's connection box and starts to disconnect. As he takes the white neutral off its connector, the kitchen's ceiling lights, which are on circuit 11, go out.

c3.title: Moving an inverter air-conditioner in Liguanea
c3.text: Dr Annette Lewis's dental clinic in Liguanea, St Andrew, is moving its inverter split air-conditioner from the waiting room to a new surgery. The outdoor unit goes to a new bracket, on a new circuit about 18 m long. The nameplate reads: 220–240 V, 1 phase, 50 Hz, MCA 14.5 A, MOP 25 A. A label on the outdoor unit's board cover says: 'Wait 10 minutes after switching off before opening.' Trainee leader Andre and two trainees do the electrical work; Mr Barrington Walters, a certified refrigeration technician, does the pipework and refrigerant.

c4.title: A grinder motor at a Seaforth spice works
c4.text: A spice-grinding works in Seaforth, St Thomas, is replacing the motor on its pimento grinder. The works has a three-phase supply of 400 V between lines, as its board schedule shows. The new motor's nameplate reads: 230 V Δ / 400 V Y, 50 Hz, 7.5 kW, 26.0 / 15.0 A, mass 62 kg, with an eye bolt on top. The starter has an overload relay adjustable from 12 to 32 A. Trainee leader Kerry-Ann and two trainees disconnect the old motor and fit the new one; the instructor will give the bump test.

c5.title: Ceiling fans and lights in a Lucea church
c5.text: A church in Lucea, Hanover, is replacing six old ceiling fans with new 132 cm fans that weigh 9 kg each, and two metal-bodied fluorescent fittings with metal LED panels. All of them are on 110 V circuits, controlled by wall switches. Trainee leader Damion and two trainees work from a mobile tower. Two of the old fans hang from plastic light-fitting boxes, each held up by one wood screw. The box for one of the fluorescent fittings has no earth conductor in it.

questions.q: What should Tashoya do about the 60 Hz rating on the replacement motor?
o: Fit it, since the voltage matches and frequency only affects clocks
Check with the supplier or maker that it is fit for 50 Hz first
Fit it, as a 60 Hz motor will simply run a little faster on 50 Hz
Fit it, and turn the overload relay down to allow for the frequency
questions.why: Jamaica's supply is 50 Hz. A 60 Hz motor on 50 Hz runs about one-sixth slower, so the pump delivers less, and at the same voltage it carries more magnetic flux, draws more current and can overheat. Use a motor rated for 50 Hz (or 50/60 Hz), or get the maker's written approval.

questions.q: A 50 Hz motor of the same 115/230 V design is found. How must its main winding halves be connected for the farm's 220 V supply?
o: In parallel, so that each half of the winding gets the full supply
In series, as the nameplate diagram shows for the higher voltage
One half only, with the other half left disconnected and taped
In series to start, then switched to parallel by the centrifugal switch
questions.why: For the higher voltage the two halves are joined in series, so each gets about half the supply. Connected in parallel on 220 V, each half would get twice its rated voltage, draw a huge current and burn out. Follow the connection diagram on the plate or inside the terminal cover.

questions.q: Mr Gayle wants the job done at once, but the motor change will take most of the morning. What is the best plan?
o: Start at once, as the work order is signed and the birds can wait a while
Leave the old motor's cable live, so the new motor can be tried quickly
Agree a start time, and have the drinkers filled before it
Wait until the next rainy day, when the birds will need less water
questions.why: Users must be able to plan for being without the equipment. Agreeing the time and filling the drinkers first protects the birds, and the work can then be done properly under full isolation, without pressure to cut corners.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the lights went out, and what should Kemoy do now?
o: Circuits 9 and 11 share a neutral; isolate 11 too and retest
The lights' breaker happened to trip; reset it and carry on with the fan job
The lamps failed by chance; finish the fan and report the lights afterwards
Circuit 9 also feeds the lights; switch it back on to see if they return
questions.why: Opening the neutral broke the return path for the lights, so the neutral is shared (borrowed). The loose end that runs to the lights can now be live at 110 V through the lamps. Isolate circuit 11 too, prove dead again, and report the shared neutral so it can be corrected.

questions.q: The fryer's cable has been disconnected at both ends and its ends boxed. What should the circuit chart now say for circuit 7?
o: Fryer, 30 A, left as it was in case a fryer is fitted again
Circuit 7 removed from the chart, with the old line crossed out
Gas range, so the chart matches what is in the kitchen now
SPARE: fryer removed, cable disconnected, the date and initials
questions.why: The chart must show the truth, so the next electrician isolates the right circuit and does not assume a load or a live cable that is no longer there. Mark it spare, say what was done and when, and remove or blank the breaker as the job requires.

questions.q: The fan's existing cable is about 1.5 m too short for the new position. Which way of extending it is acceptable?
o: Join it in the ceiling space with connectors wrapped well in tape
Solder the joint, cover it with sleeving and plaster it into the wall
Join it with proper connectors in a covered box that stays accessible
Fit a plug and socket above the ceiling so the fan can be unplugged
questions.why: Every joint must be made with suitable connectors inside a box with a cover that can still be reached for inspection. Tape-wrapped joints loosen and overheat, buried joints cannot be found or checked, and a hidden plug and socket is not a proper fixed-wiring joint.

questions.q: Andre has locked off the outdoor unit and proved dead at its terminal block. What must happen before anyone touches the inverter board?
o: Nothing more, as proving dead at the terminal block covers the board
Short the large capacitor with an insulated screwdriver to empty it
Wait until the indoor unit's display goes out, then start at once
Wait at least 10 minutes, then measure the DC capacitor voltage
questions.why: Inverter boards have large DC capacitors that stay charged after the supply is off, and the terminal block test does not measure them. Wait the time on the label, then measure across the capacitor on a suitable DC range before you touch anything. Shorting it can cause an arc, burns and damage.

questions.q: Using the nameplate, which breaker and cable suit the new circuit?
o: A 15 A single-pole breaker with 14 AWG copper cable
A 20 A two-pole breaker with 12 AWG copper cable
A 32 A two-pole breaker, the size just above the MOP
A 40 A two-pole breaker, so the inverter never trips it
questions.why: The cable must be rated for at least the MCA (14.5 A) and the breaker must not exceed the MOP (25 A). A 20 A two-pole breaker on 12 AWG copper meets both, and opens both 110 V lines. A single-pole breaker would leave one line live; 32 A and 40 A are above the maker's maximum.

questions.q: Each conductor of the 18 m run of 12 AWG cable has 0.0052 Ω per metre. About what is the voltage drop when the unit draws 14.5 A?
o: About 1.4 V
About 5.4 V
About 2.7 V
About 27 V
questions.why: The current flows out and back, so the loop is 2 × 18 = 36 m. Resistance = 36 × 0.0052 = 0.187 Ω, and VD = 14.5 × 0.187 = about 2.7 V, roughly 1.2% of 220 V: well inside a 3% aim. 1.4 V counts only one conductor.

questions.q: Before the insulation resistance test on the new circuit, what should Andre do about the outdoor unit?
o: Disconnect the unit, so the 500 V test does not reach its electronics
Switch the unit on, so its contactor closes and every part is tested
Nothing, as the unit's inverter board is built to take 500 V DC
Bridge line to earth inside the unit, so the reading comes out higher
questions.why: An insulation resistance tester applies 500 V DC, which can damage inverter boards and other electronics and give false low readings. Test the fixed wiring with the unit disconnected, or follow the maker's advice for testing the unit itself.

questions.q: How should Kerry-Ann set the links in the new motor's terminal box?
o: In delta, because delta always gives a motor its full rated power
In star for starting, then change them by hand to delta for running
In delta, because the lower voltage on the plate is the safer choice
In star, because the works' supply is 400 V between lines
questions.why: The plate says the motor is connected in star (Y) for 400 V and in delta (Δ) for 230 V. On a 400 V supply in delta, each winding would get 400 V instead of 230 V, draw a very high current and burn out. Star-delta starting needs a special starter, not links changed by hand.

questions.q: To what current should the overload relay be set for this motor on this supply?
o: 15.0 A, the current the plate gives for the star connection
26.0 A, the larger current on the plate, to avoid nuisance trips
32 A, the top of the dial, so that the grinder never stops
20.5 A, halfway between the two nameplate currents
questions.why: Connected in star on 400 V, the motor draws 15.0 A at full load, so the relay is set to that figure (or as the maker or code allows). Set at 26 A or more, it would let the motor overheat for a long time without tripping.

questions.q: What is the right way to lift the new 62 kg motor onto the grinder's base?
o: Two trainees lift it by its shaft and fan cover, one on each end
A hoist on the eye bolt, screwed fully home, lifting the motor alone
The hoist lifts the motor and grinder together by the motor's eye bolt
One strong trainee lifts it, keeping it close to his body
questions.why: 62 kg is too heavy for one person, and the shaft and fan cover are not lifting points. A motor's eye bolt is made to carry the motor's own weight, screwed fully home, and must never be used to lift the motor with the machine it drives.

questions.q: At the bump test the grinder turns the wrong way. What is the correct fix?
o: Change the links from star to delta to make the motor reverse
Swap the earth and one line conductor at the motor terminals
Isolate it, then swap any two of the three lines at the motor
Run it the wrong way, as a grinder works in either direction
questions.why: Swapping any two of the three line conductors reverses the rotating field, so the motor turns the other way. Do it only with the motor isolated, locked and proved dead. Changing the links alters the voltage the windings get, and the earth must never carry current.

questions.q: What must be done about the two old fan positions held by plastic light-fitting boxes?
o: Fit fan-rated boxes or braces, fixed to the structure
Add a second wood screw to each box, as two screws hold 9 kg
Hang the new fans from the boxes, with their safety cables tied
Use the same boxes, since the new fans are lighter than the old
questions.why: A fan's weight, wobble and twisting force are too much for an ordinary light-fitting box. The fan must hang from a box or bracket made and marked for fan support, fixed firmly to the building's structure.

questions.q: Damion finds that one fan's wall switch breaks the white (neutral) conductor, although the fan still stops when it is switched off. Why must this be corrected?
o: The fan will run slowly, because the neutral carries half the current
The fan stays live when switched off, so cleaning it can give a shock
The switch will burn out, because a neutral carries a higher voltage
The breaker will trip each time the switch is turned off and on
questions.why: With the switch in the neutral, the fan's motor and wiring stay connected to the live line even when the fan is off. Someone cleaning or repairing it could get a shock. The switch must always break the line conductor.

questions.q: The box for one LED panel has no earth conductor, and the panel has a metal body. What should Damion do?
o: Connect the panel's earth lead to the neutral in the box
Fit the panel, as LED panels draw too little current to matter
Stop that panel until a protective conductor is run to the box
Fit the panel and tape over its earth terminal to keep it tidy
questions.why: A metal-bodied fitting needs a protective conductor, so that a fault trips the breaker instead of leaving the body live. Joining earth to neutral is dangerous: the body would carry neutral current and could become live if the neutral breaks.

questions.q: A 3.8 kW, 220 V storage water heater is to replace a 3 kW one on a 20 A two-pole circuit wired in 12 AWG copper. Treating the heater as a continuous load, what is needed?
o: Nothing: 17.3 A is below the 20 A breaker rating
A 25 A breaker, keeping the existing 12 AWG cable
A 40 A breaker with 8 AWG, twice the heater's current
At least a 25 A two-pole breaker with 10 AWG cable
questions.why: 3,800 ÷ 220 = 17.3 A, and 17.3 × 1.25 = 21.6 A, which is more than 20 A. The next breaker size is 25 A, and 12 AWG copper is limited to 20 A, so the cable must be upgraded too (10 AWG). Changing only the breaker would leave the cable unprotected.

questions.q: With a cooker isolated, a trainee tests a hob ring marked 1,800 W, 220 V with an ohmmeter. Which reading shows the ring is sound?
o: About 8.2 Ω
About 26.9 Ω
About 122 Ω
About 0.12 Ω
questions.why: R = V² ÷ P = 220 × 220 ÷ 1,800 = 48,400 ÷ 1,800 = 26.9 Ω. Nickel-chrome wire changes little with heat, so the cold reading should be close. 8.2 A is the current (1,800 ÷ 220), not a resistance.

questions.q: A trainee has labelled every conductor on a motor but has not photographed or sketched the terminal box links. Which hold point should catch this?
o: The check of the dead test results before the supply is restored
The bump test, when the instructor sees which way the motor turns
The handover, when the operator signs to accept the job
The connection record check, before disconnecting
questions.why: The record must be complete before anything comes off, because once the links are removed nobody can be sure how they were. Catching it at the right hold point saves a damaged motor; later checks would be too late.
